summary: Specifies how the iCalendar Transport-independent Interoperability Protocol is carried over Internet email. It lets calendar invitations travel as ordinary mail messages. It is a proposed standard that was replaced by RFC 6047.

eli5.summary: It is a way to send meeting invitations inside regular email, so any email program can pass them along.

questions: how are calendar invitations sent by email
subtitle: A way to send calendar invitations and scheduling information through email.

tldr.problem: Calendar applications need to send meeting invitations, updates, and responses via email, but email systems do not know how to recognize or handle calendar data.
tldr.mechanism: iMIP (iCalendar Message-Based Interoperability Protocol) defines a binding that packages calendar objects as email attachments with the MIME type text/calendar, including method identifiers so recipients know what action to take.
tldr.outcome: Calendar invitations could be sent as regular email messages, allowing any email client to participate in calendar exchanges. RFC 2447 was replaced by RFC 6047 which updated the specification.

today: RFC 2447 was a Proposed Standard and has been superseded by RFC 6047. The core idea of sending calendar objects via email with the text/calendar MIME type remains central to calendar interoperability on the Internet.

sections.title: Calendar Scheduling Over Email
sections.content:
iMIP is the iCalendar Message-Based Interoperability Protocol. It specifies how to bind iCalendar objects (a standard format for calendar data) to Internet email transport using MIME (Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions).

iMIP is built on two related standards: iCalendar (RFC 2445), which defines the format for calendar events, to-dos, and journal entries, and iTIP (RFC 2446), which defines a transport-independent scheduling protocol using methods like REQUEST, REPLY, and PUBLISH. iMIP takes this iTIP protocol and carries it over SMTP and email.

With iMIP, a calendar user can send a meeting invitation to another calendar user as an ordinary email message, and that message can be processed automatically by calendar applications that understand the format.
sections.eli5: iMIP is a way to send meeting invitations inside regular email. The invitation is formatted so calendar programs can read it and automatically understand what they should do: add the meeting to your calendar, let you accept or decline, or update an existing meeting.

sections.title: Roles and Components
sections.content:
iMIP messages involve two primary roles: the Organizer (who arranges the event) and Attendees (who participate). An iMIP message can contain calendar components such as VEVENT (events), VTODO (tasks), or VJOURNAL (notes).

The scheduling protocol defines several methods that identify the message type: REQUEST asks attendees to participate, REPLY sends back an acceptance or decline, PUBLISH announces information without expecting responses, CANCEL withdraws an earlier invitation, and others.

Important: the RFC-822 Sender or Reply-To headers do not reliably indicate the organizer or attendees. Calendar programs must read the actual text/calendar body part and examine the ORGANIZER and ATTENDEE properties to determine who the participants are.
sections.eli5: Every iMIP message has a sender (usually the meeting organizer) and attendees. The message says what action to take: REQUEST means come to this meeting, REPLY means I will or will not attend, and PUBLISH means here is information.

sections.title: Email Binding and Content Type
sections.content:
An iMIP message must have a Content-Type header of text/calendar. The header must include a method parameter with the same value as the METHOD property inside the calendar object. Optionally, a component parameter identifies the calendar component type (such as vevent or vtodo).

Example header: Content-Type:text/calendar; method=REQUEST; charset=UTF-8; component=vevent

The RFC recommends that messages include a charset parameter if the calendar contains non-ASCII characters; UTF-8 is the default for iCalendar. Messages that contain multiple calendar objects with different methods must use multipart/mixed encapsulation so each object has its own text/calendar part.

To make invitations readable by email clients that do not understand text/calendar, messages SHOULD use multipart/alternative to include both a plain-text description and the full calendar object.
sections.eli5: iMIP messages are formatted as email attachments with the label text/calendar. The email also says whether the message is a REQUEST, REPLY, or other type. If the invitation has a lot of non-English characters, the email says which encoding it uses.

sections.title: Authentication and Authorization
sections.content:
iMIP messages must defend against two main spoofing threats: someone claiming to be the organizer of a meeting, or someone claiming to accept or decline on behalf of an attendee.

The RFC requires implementations to sign and encrypt text/calendar attachments using RFC 1847 (Security Multiparts for MIME), which defines multipart/signed and multipart/encrypted. This allows recipients to authenticate the message sender and verify that the organizer or attendee authorized the request.

Authorization rules are strict: only the organizer of an event can modify or cancel it; only an attendee can send a reply for that attendee. The sent-by parameter allows one calendar user to work on behalf of another, but implementations must provide mechanisms for users to approve or deny delegation requests.
sections.eli5: iMIP messages need to be signed (so you know who really sent it) and can be encrypted (so only the intended recipient sees it). Only the meeting organizer can change or cancel the meeting, and only attendees can say whether they will come.

sections.title: Message Examples
sections.content:
The RFC includes six examples of iMIP messages:

Single component with attachment: A meeting invitation with a reference to an external document (ftp URL).

Multipart alternative: The same invitation sent twice: once as plain text for simple email clients, and once as a full iCalendar object.

Inline attachment: An invitation with a Content-ID reference to a document included in the same message (using multipart/related).

Multiple similar components: Several events in one message (company picnic and bowling tournament) using a single iCalendar object with multiple VEVENT blocks.

Multiple mixed components: An event and a to-do in the same message, requiring multipart/mixed encapsulation because they have different component types.

Detailed components: A meeting invitation with attendees, time zones, and an attached document, using multipart/related and multipart/alternative.
sections.eli5: iMIP can send a single meeting invitation, multiple meetings, or meetings mixed with to-do lists. Invitations can include plain-text versions for simple email programs, or attachments that are embedded in the message.
